title: The Friday night bag
note: Fictional patient. Values are illustrative; your PD program’s pathway and the nephrologist’s orders come first.
intro: You are the PD nurse on call. At 21:10 on Friday, Mr. Danilo Cruz, 56, on continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD) for two years, calls. His evening drain bag is cloudy and his belly is a little sore. “I’ll just throw it away and see if the next one clears,” he says. “I can come in on Monday.”

n1.prompt: What do you tell him first?

choices.text: Possible peritonitis: keep the bag, don’t wait, and answer some questions now.
choices.feedback: Cloudy effluent with abdominal pain meets the clinical criterion. Every cloudy bag is possible peritonitis until the team says otherwise. The bag is the sample the laboratory needs.

choices.text: Fine: throw it away and call if the next bag is still cloudy.
choices.feedback: Discarding the bag loses the first sample, and waiting lets peritonitis advance. Peritonitis is a leading reason patients lose PD as a therapy.
choices.then: You call back five minutes later and ask him to keep the bag. He had not thrown it away yet.

choices.text: Ask him to keep the bag in the refrigerator and bring it in on Monday morning, when the PD unit can test it.
choices.feedback: Keeping the bag is right, but empirical antibiotics should start as soon as possible after sampling. Two days is too long.
choices.then: You reconsider and go through the screening questions with him.

vitals.screen: Rigors, vomited twice, faint on standing

n2.scene: He takes his temperature: 38.6 °C. He has been shaking with chills, has vomited twice, cannot keep water down, and felt faint when he stood up to get the thermometer.

choices.text: Emergency department now with the bag; call the nephrologist and alert the ED.
choices.feedback: Rigors, vomiting that stops him drinking, and faintness are signs of instability. They take him to emergency care tonight, not to the PD unit in the morning.

choices.text: Come to the PD unit first thing tomorrow with the bag, where the team knows him and can sample the effluent properly.
choices.feedback: That would suit a stable patient. He is not stable, so the emergency pathway applies tonight.
choices.then: You change the plan: emergency department now, nephrologist informed.

choices.text: Take paracetamol, drink slowly, and call back in two hours.
choices.feedback: Paracetamol hides the fever without treating the cause, and he cannot keep fluids down. Two hours lost in an unstable patient matters.
choices.then: You change the plan: emergency department now, nephrologist informed.

n3.scene: He arrives with the bag. The emergency physician asks you by phone whether to wait for the cell count before starting antibiotics.
n3.prompt: What do you advise, within your role?

choices.text: Send count, Gram stain, and culture labeled with dwell and time, then start antibiotics.
choices.feedback: Samples before antibiotics when feasible, but sampling must not delay treatment. Empirical therapy covers both gram-positive and gram-negative organisms; choice and dose are the prescriber’s.

choices.text: Wait for the cell count to confirm peritonitis before giving antibiotics, so he is not treated for something he may not have.
choices.feedback: In an unstable patient with cloudy effluent and pain, treatment starts as soon as samples are taken. The count confirms the diagnosis; it does not gate the first dose.
choices.then: The emergency physician starts the ordered antibiotics after sampling.

choices.text: Give antibiotics immediately; skip the samples, since he is unwell.
choices.feedback: Speed is right, but taking the samples takes minutes and tells the team which organism to treat. Sample first when it does not delay care.
choices.then: The effluent is sampled within minutes and the antibiotics follow.

n4.scene: On Monday he is on an aminoglycoside per the nephrologist’s order. His effluent is clearing. In passing he says his ears have been ringing since yesterday.

choices.text: Report the ringing today, ask about hearing and balance, and keep tracking results.
choices.feedback: Aminoglycosides can damage hearing. Many patients do not mention it unless asked. The decision about the antibiotic is the prescriber’s; your report makes it possible.

choices.text: Reassure him that ringing ears are common with fever and should settle as the infection clears.
choices.feedback: Ringing in the ears on an aminoglycoside is a warning sign of ototoxicity, which can be permanent. Report it the same day.

choices.text: Tell him to skip tonight’s antibiotic dose until his ears settle.
choices.feedback: Stopping or changing an antibiotic is the prescriber’s decision. An unplanned gap can let the infection relapse.

n5.scene: The culture grew an enteric organism. At the review visit you learn that his cat sleeps in the room where he does exchanges, he takes an over-the-counter acid reducer for heartburn, his last potassium was low, and he often goes three days without a bowel movement.

choices.text: Retrain, move the cat out, report the acid reducer and potassium, and involve the dietitian.
choices.feedback: Every episode gets a review without blame. Pets in the exchange area, low potassium, and H2-receptor blockers are modifiable risk factors named in the 2022 ISPD update; constipation is linked to enteric episodes. Medicines are the prescriber’s to change.

choices.text: Tell him to stop the acid reducer and eat more bananas for his potassium, then retrain his exchange technique.
choices.feedback: Both are prescriber and dietitian decisions. Report them; do not change medicines or diet on your own.

choices.text: Retrain his exchange technique and close the episode.
choices.feedback: Retraining is standard after peritonitis, but this episode was enteric. The cat, the acid reducer, the low potassium, and the constipation are the findings that prevent the next one.

end.title: Episode closed
end.text: He completes the course with clear effluent and his hearing is reviewed. You record the times from call to sample to first dose, the episode classification, and the follow-up plan, and the episode is counted in the program’s peritonitis rate.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Every cloudy bag is possible peritonitis. Keep the bag; do not wait.
  • Screen for instability: rigors, vomiting, faintness, confusion, severe pain mean emergency care now.
  • Sample, then treat without delay. Label dwell time and collection time.
  • Ask about hearing on aminoglycosides, and report it.
  • Every episode gets a review: technique, pets, acid reducers, low potassium, constipation.

See The first hour and Prevention after every episode.
